sources.news_title: Trump bails on Blanche to save his own ass
sources.text:
President Donald Trump is officially turning against his own party.
On Thursday, he went off on a pair of GOP senators, attacking them for refusing to confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general unless Trump gives up his corrupt “settlement” with the Internal Revenue Service that would shield him and his family from any audits or prosecutions.
“Todd Blanche is a STAR, and everyone knows it! He has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “However, John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting.”
He then threatened to temporarily withdraw Blanche’s nomination until the end of their terms.
“Remember, both Cornyn and Tillis voted for Merrick Garland, and others, too numerous to mention. I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office,” he added.
The fact that Trump is so willing to give up on Blanche’s confirmation rather than agree to drop his settlement with the IRS shows just how nervous he is of being prosecuted for his and his family’s corruption.
The settlement is, in essence, a preemptive pardon for himself and for “related or affiliated individuals (including, without limitation, family or others filing jointly), or parties including trusts, parent, sister, or related companies, affiliates, and subsidiaries.”
The utterly corrupt deal that Blanche helped Trump orchestrate with the IRS is so bad that even GOP senators are balking at it, with Cornyn and Tillis doubling down on denying Blanche’s nomination until the settlement is dropped.
Of course, Cornyn won’t admit that it’s Trump blocking the way, but come on—who else would it be?
“If this were just between me and Todd Blanche, we would have worked this out, but, apparently, he’s getting some pushback from higher ups at the White House,” Cornyn told reporters Thursday. “I don’t know who, but it doesn’t need to be this hard.”
But Cornyn did fire back at Trump for suggesting that he and Tillis are the only senators who are uncomfortable with the corrupt IRS settlement.
“POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis,” Cornyn responded to Trump’s Truth Social post.
Related | Trump’s Texas Senate endorsement is coming back to bite him
As for Trump’s plan to wait out Cornyn and Tillis’ terms to get Blanche confirmed, well, that’s a risky and stupid bet in itself.
Republicans could lose their House majority in the midterms amid growing backlash and frustration with Trump over his boondoggle of a war in Iran that’s spiking gas prices and threatening to take down the global economy.
Indeed, Tillis is likely to be replaced by Democratic candidate Roy Cooper, former governor of North Carolina. And Cornyn’s seat is also in danger, as the Trump-backed, scandal-plagued GOP nominee Ken Paxton is unpalatable to many Republican voters.
“There’s a good chance at least one—if not both—will be replaced by a Democrat instead of a more amenable Republican,” Cook Political Report editor Jessica Taylor wrote on X.
If Democrats take control of the Senate, Blanche will have no chance in hell of being confirmed.
But, of course, Trump doesn’t care about anyone but himself. And a shady immunity deal is definitely more valuable to him than any attorney general.

sources.news_title: Trump says he ‘may’ pull Blanche AG nomination temporarily
sources.text:
President Trump says he is willing to pull Todd Blanche‘s nomination for attorney general. The news comes as two key Republicans are withholding their support over concerns about the Justice Department’s deal with President Trump to end his IRS lawsuit.
Trump said Thursday he was willing to end the nomination, but he was by no means conciliatory in his tone, saying he would keep Blanche on as acting attorney general and renominate him later. In addition, Trump took aim at the two Republican senators withholding their support — John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, both of whose support Blanche would need to advance in his nomination in committee.
“I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office,” Trump wrote in a social media post.
Both Cornyn and Tillis are leaving Congress in January. Tillis announced his retirement last year, after publicly clashing with Trump over his massive tax-and-spending bill. Cornyn lost his primary this year to a Trump-backed challenger.
In his post, Trump bragged that both senators’ “political careers have been ended by my action.”
Blanche, Trump’s former personal lawyer, has been a contentious pick to lead the Justice Department amid questions about his handling of the Epstein files, the targeting of Trump’s political foes and the broader politicization of justice.
Tillis and Cornyn this week voiced their opposition to Blanche over an agreement the Justice Department struck to end President Trump’s IRS lawsuit over his leaked tax returns.
The settlement included the creation of a nearly $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund, which Cornyn and Tillis have vocally opposed for weeks. That fund would compensate people who alleged they were unfairly targeted by the government, meaning money could have gone to defendants charged with wrongdoing in the Jan. 6 riots.
A second, related part was a sweeping immunity deal for Trump, his family and businesses from audits of past tax returns.
Blanche has said the fund is not moving forward, but Cornyn and Tillis wanted written guarantees from the Justice Department about the scope of the tax immunity deal — guarantees that they said the DOJ would not provide.
“For some reason, I don’t know whether it’s the staff of the DOJ or who it is, but they simply, they know what they need to do, but they simply refuse to do it,” Cornyn told reporters this week.
In response to Trump’s Thursday post, Cornyn responded with his own post: “POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis.”
Democrats have been united in opposition to his nomination, while Republicans have, by and large, been supportive.
In addition to criticizing the anti-weaponization fund, Tillis had also been vocal in criticizing Blanche’s handling of the scandal around the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Late Wednesday, the Senate Judiciary Committee chairman, GOP Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, announced the planned vote on Blanche was postponed as work continues to secure sufficient support for his nomination.
While Trump says he would renominate Blanche once Cornyn and Tillis are gone from the Senate, that plan would be far more difficult if Democrats win the Senate in November — a distinct possibility given this year’s map and Trump’s low approval ratings.

sources.news_title: Trump might pause Blanche nomination as GOP senators object to IRS lawsuit settlement
sources.text:
Trump might pause Blanche nomination as GOP senators object to IRS lawsuit settlement
-    Click here to listen to this article 
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Two outgoing Senate Republicans are threatening to sink President Trump’s choice for attorney general, Todd Blanche, unless the Justice Department unwinds a controversial $1.8‑billion settlement fund and narrows his tax immunity.
- Trump has publicly attacked Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis and is mulling withdrawing Blanche’s nomination, a move that could backfire if Democrats cut into Republicans’ slim Senate majority this fall.
The high-stakes nomination of Todd Blanche to be attorney general has turned into a clash of wills between President Trump and two Senate Republicans whose political careers he claims credit for ending.
After a vote on Blanche’s nomination was delayed over concerns raised by two lame-duck Republican senators, the president said Thursday he might put Blanche’s nomination on hold rather than meet their demands.
Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) have indicated that they will vote to support advancing Blanche’s nomination only if the Justice Department provides written assurance that it has completely abandoned a controversial $1.8-billion “anti-weaponization” fund created as part of a settlement between Trump and the Internal Revenue Service and will limit the scope of tax audit immunity granted to Trump, his sons and a business.
Those provisions were part of a proposed settlement of a $10-billion lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS, which is part of his administration.
“The opposition to such a high-ranking executive branch nomination from within Republican ranks is quite unprecedented,” said Phil Brest, who was a top Democratic staffer for the Senate Judiciary Committee during the nominations of Jeff Sessions, Bill Barr and Merrick Garland, who each served as attorney general.
The Senate careers of both Cornyn and TIllis are coming to an end this year after Trump declined to endorse them.
“John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, his social media platform. “I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office.”
The former Trump defense attorney has been leading the Justice Department on an interim basis since Atty. Gen. Pam Bondi was fired in April.
But that decision brings about its own political risk.
With the president’s approval rating sitting below 35% in recent polls, Democrats could shrink or even reverse the Republican Party’s current 53-seat Senate majority this November. Cornyn‘s and Tillis’ seats in Texas and North Carolina are both at risk of flipping to Democrats.
“So waiting until 2027 could be far harder than it is right now,” said Jessica Taylor, the Senate and governors editor at the nonpartisan Cook Political Report.
Blanche has been serving as acting attorney general since Atty. Gen Pam Bondi was fired in April. He was previously the deputy attorney general and has been associated with some of the most controversial policies associated with the Trump administration, including the IRS settlement, the handling of the Epstein files and prosecutions of Trump’s perceived enemies.
Blanche can continue in the acting role even if he is not confirmed, but the Trump administration would be blocked from appointing a new deputy attorney general unless he is confirmed.
Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, which is vetting Blanche, told reporters Thursday that he is hoping to keep Blanche’s nomination on track.
“I’m going to work real hard the next few days to get this thing settled. That’s what we’re going to do. I’m not going to consider any other option, because there’s no reason to consider other options at this point,” Grassley said.
Because the Senate is scheduled to begin its five-week August recess at the end of next week, Blanche probably wouldn’t come before the full Senate for a vote until September at the earliest if the nomination advances out of the Judiciary Committee.
That would put the vote squarely in the middle of peak campaign season, which could present vulnerable Republicans such as Sen. Susan Collins of Maine and Sen. Dan Sullivan of Alaska with a difficult vote on a nominee who has been linked to many of the Trump administration’s most polarizing policies.
A vote against Blanche could incur the wrath of Trump, while a vote for him could turn off moderate voters.
“It’s a Catch-22 for a lot of these candidates. They still need Trump’s voters to come out, but they still need a swing vote as well,” Taylor said.
Blanche worked earlier in his career as a federal prosecutor in New York but was more recently Trump’s criminal defense attorney in the lead-up to his second term in the White House.
The economic pain many Americans feel after years of stagnant wages and steep inflation is unlikely to lift before the November elections, and could be a major liability for Republicans, according to political and economic experts.
Blanche faced questions about his independence from his former client throughout his nomination hearing earlier this month. But his answer to one seemingly friendly question, about whether he and Trump are friends, might have inadvertently hurt his case.
“I’m his lawyer,” Blanche replied, before correcting himself. “Was his lawyer.”
The Judiciary Committee currently has 12 Republicans and 10 Democrats. With all 10 Democrats firmly in opposition to Blanche, a vote against moving forward by Cornyn or Tillis would probably put an end to the nomination.
This isn’t the first time Tillis has wielded his political leverage during a high-stakes nomination process.
He briefly blocked the nomination of Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh until the Justice Department dropped a lawsuit against outgoing Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell.
“Sen. Tillis has been unafraid to use his vote to extract concessions from the Trump administration,” said Brest, who is now president of the American Constitution Society, a progressive legal nonprofit. “There’s a playbook for this and he has been effective with that playbook.”

Republican North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis accused President Donald Trump of taking “bad advice” after Trump threatened to withdraw acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination.
The Senate Judiciary Committee postponed a vote Thursday on Blanche’s nomination to serve permanently as attorney general after Tillis and Republican Texas Sen. John Cornyn opposed advancing it.
Neither senator will return next Congress. Tillis announced his retirement in June 2025, while Cornyn lost his Republican primary after Trump endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the closing stages of the race. (RELATED: Trump AG Nominee’s Confirmation In Limbo)
Trump threatened to withdraw Blanche’s nomination and resubmit it after Tillis and Cornyn leave office in January.
Speaking with reporters on Capitol Hill, Tillis suggested to CNN Chief Congressional Correspondent Manu Raju that the president wanted to preserve the possibility of reviving a proposed anti-weaponization compensation fund. Tillis and Cornyn have said they will not support Blanche without written assurances that the fund is dead.
“The president’s getting bad advice,” Tillis said. “He should listen to Blanche and others who think if it’s dead, it should be rendered completely dead.”

sources.news_title: Trump threatens to pull Todd Blanche’s nomination for U.S. Attorney-General as Senate standoff escalates
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump threatened on Thursday to withdraw until next year his nomination of Todd Blanche to serve as U.S. Attorney-General, escalating a standoff with Senate Republicans who have objected to a proposed “anti-weaponization” fund that could benefit his allies.
The dispute highlights Trump’s weakening grip on a Congress controlled by his own party, but it does not affect the tenure of Blanche, who can continue to head the Justice Department as acting Attorney-General. Republican Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis have held up Blanche’s nomination while seeking written assurances that the Justice Department will not set up the US$1.8-billion “anti-weaponization” program. Trump critics have derided it as a slush fund to reward supporters with taxpayer money.
Cornyn and Tillis met with Blanche together for 45 minutes late Thursday afternoon to try to salvage the confirmation vote, according to a person familiar with the matter. The person, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the two sides are working “collaboratively,” are closer to an agreement and that Blanche answered questions about his proposed resolution.
Trump said on social media that he could withdraw Blanche’s nomination and then renominate him next year after Cornyn and Tillis have left office. Trump also claimed credit for ending the careers of the two senators.
“Todd Blanche is a STAR, and everyone knows it! He has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney-Generals of All Time,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. “I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office.”
GOP senators threaten to block Trump’s pick for Attorney-General over controversial IRS settlement
Cornyn and Tillis are due to end their terms in the Senate in early January. Blanche, Trump’s former personal lawyer, was named acting Attorney-General after the president fired Pam Bondi in April.
The stalemate over Blanche’s nomination is the latest sign of a growing rupture between Trump and some Senate Republicans. The party faces the possibility of losing its 53-47 seat majority in the Senate in November’s midterm elections, and some Republicans in the chamber have shown an increasing willingness to resist the president.
Republicans have turned away efforts to fund Trump’s ballroom on the site of the demolished White House East Wing, and resisted his calls to change Senate rules to pass his partisan voter ID bill, the SAVE America Act. Cornyn, who lost his primary re-election bid in Texas after Trump endorsed challenger Ken Paxton, told reporters that negotiations were likely over until next week. Tillis, who represents North Carolina, announced his retirement last year after clashing with Trump over Medicaid cuts in the president’s sweeping tax cut and spending bill.
Cornyn and Tillis have been the public faces of opposition to Trump. But Cornyn said on social media that other senators share their concerns.
Blanche has also met with Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah to try to shore up support.
Blanche likely does not need to be confirmed to effectively serve as Trump’s Attorney-General for the rest of his term as president. Acting officers can serve in their roles “for the period that the nomination is pending in the Senate,” so long as their nomination is not formally rejected or withdrawn.
And as deputy Attorney-General, he can exercise all duties of the Attorney-General’s office when that office is vacant. That means that so long as he is in that position, and there is no one above him, Blanche can likely run the Justice Department indefinitely.
The “anti-weaponization” fund, crafted as part of a legal settlement between Trump and the Justice Department to resolve his US$10-billion lawsuit against the IRS over allegedly mishandling his tax records, was put on hold amid opposition from Republicans in Congress.
The fund could benefit Trump allies who have said they were unfairly targeted in the past by the federal government for their involvement in the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Trump last year gave clemency to his supporters who were prosecuted for their roles in the Jan. six riot.
Cornyn told reporters earlier on Thursday that he was still waiting for the Justice Department to formalize assurances that it would not implement the fund.
“I don’t know whether they think they can wait us out or we’ll cave. But I can assure you we won’t,” Cornyn told reporters.
Cornyn and Tillis also have objections to a deal with the Internal Revenue Service that would prevent tax audits of Trump and his associates.
Trump ousted Bondi over his frustrations with her performance, especially over the release of files relating to the late financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Trump also felt Bondi was not moving quickly enough to prosecute critics and adversaries whom he wanted to face criminal charges, according to sources.

sources.news_title: Trump suggests pulling AG nomination amid Cornyn concerns
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Thursday floated pulling his nominee for attorney general until Sen. John Cornyn is out of office, escalating tensions between the two as the Texas Republican continues to insist on changes to a deal protecting Trump and his circle from tax audits.
Cornyn and Sen. Thom Tillis, R-North Carolina, have held up acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination in the Senate Judiciary Committee over their shared concerns about a settlement between Trump and the Department of Justice that created a $1.8 billion fund to pay out victims of the agency’s alleged weaponization and gave Trump and his family immunity from being audited by the Internal Revenue Service. Their demands to tweak those provisions remained unmet by the panel’s scheduled Thursday morning vote on Blanche, forcing its postponement.
Amid the impasse, Trump weighed in on social media, suggesting he could put Blanche’s nomination on ice until 2027 rather than acquiesce to Cornyn and Tillis’ demands. Cornyn is serving out the final months of his term after losing his primary reelection bid to Attorney General Ken Paxton, whom Trump endorsed after Cornyn and his allies spent months courting the president’s backing.
“Todd Blanche is a STAR, and everyone knows it!” Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday morning. “He has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time. However, John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee.”
In holding up Blanche’s nomination, Cornyn has sought to codify the acting agency head’s word that the “anti-weaponization fund” is dead, insisting that it be made legally unenforceable. And he has said the audit shield needs to be as narrow on paper as Blanche testified it would be.
Even before Trump blasted Cornyn on social media and suggested sour grapes were at play, Cornyn dismissed the idea.
“That has nothing to do with it,” he told CNN Thursday morning. “This is about making sure that even if you’re the president of the United States, you don’t get favorable terms from the government in a settlement of a lawsuit that ordinary citizens would not get, like protection from audits by the IRS into the foreseeable future. I think this is about making sure that we maintain the integrity of our justice system and fairness for everybody involved.”
The saga began when Trump took the unusual step of suing his own government in January over the leak of his tax records in 2019 and 2020. The DOJ, representing the IRS and the Department of Treasury, settled the lawsuit in May by creating a $1.8 billion fund for alleged victims of DOJ weaponization to make claims. In an order signed by Blanche, the department also shielded Trump, his family and his business associates from tax audits.
Amidst an outcry of criticism, including from Republicans, that taxpayer money could go to Jan. 6 rioters, the DOJ backed off of the fund, declaring it a moot issue. Cornyn has maintained that he needs to see written modifications to the settlement ensuring the fund cannot be revived in any form, including through a breach of contract lawsuit from a plaintiff, such as Trump, to attempt to compel payouts. And he has sought a written guarantee that the audit shield does not provide immunity from other agency audits beyond the IRS, and that it covers only people who were parties to the lawsuit. He has also sought assurances that the shield does not apply to future tax returns or legal cases.
Cornyn said he provided the DOJ with a “redline strikeout” that would change the settlement to meet his standards, adding that the issue could be resolved swiftly if the department would agree to such language.
“I thought we were pretty close to landing the plane last night, but this morning there’s been some more complications,” he told CNN. “I think if this were just between me and Todd Blanche, we would have worked this out. But apparently he’s getting some pushback from higher ups at the White House. I don’t know who, but this doesn’t need to be this hard.”
In his post, Trump suggested that he could withdraw Blanche’s nomination, keep him on in an acting capacity through the end of the year, and then resubmit his nomination to the next Congress, when both Cornyn and Tillis, who is retiring, are gone. sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump appears willing to potentially sacrifice his handpicked nominee for attorney general in order to preserve a blatantly corrupt IRS legal settlement two key Republican senators are demanding changes to.
In a Thursday rant on his social media site, Trump ripped Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) for holding up the confirmation of Todd Blanche, his former personal attorney who negotiated the deal, suggesting he would instead pull Blanche’s nomination until a new Senate is sworn in next year.
Cornyn and Tillis are demanding changes to the IRS settlement, which grants Trump and his family immunity from IRS tax audits, in order to secure their votes for him in the Senate Judiciary Committee. The settlement also created a wildly problematic $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” to give federal payouts to people who claim they were wronged by the U.S. government, namely Jan. 6, 2021, rioters.
Cornyn, in particular, has seemed baffled by the Trump administration’s refusal to rule out a revitalization of the fund, which it killed amid blowback from Republicans earlier this year.
The committee had to postpone a vote on Blanche’s nomination earlier Thursday because, without Cornyn’s and Tillis’ support, he doesn’t have the votes to advance.
“John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting,” the president wrote. “Remember, both Cornyn and Tillis voted for Merrick Garland, and others, too numerous to mention. I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office.”
Republicans on Capitol Hill seemed caught off guard by Trump’s abrupt threat to pull Blanche’s nomination. Some were still in talks with the attorney general nominee and his team, and earlier Thursday, Tillis told colleagues he’s been “working in good faith” with Blanche to come up with parameters on Trump’s settlement deal that they can agree on.
Cornyn said he thought he had reached a deal with Blanche on Wednesday night — until Trump learned about it, and killed it.
“I think as far as Blanche and the Department of Justice, we were pretty much on the same page,” he told reporters. “But then, when the president got wind of it,” it was off.
The Texas senator said he hasn’t spoken to Trump at all this week. As for the status of his talks with Blanche going forward, Cornyn said, “It’s kind of shut down for a while.”
Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), the chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, seemed determined to find a way to advance the president’s nominee.
“We’re just working very hard to get a resolution,” he said. “I’m going to consider [Blanche] because he’s well qualified and I want to get him approved.”
Asked if he thinks Trump should yank Blanche’s nomination amid the delays, Grassley repeated that he wants to get him through.
“Why would I consider anything else?” he asked.
Flocked by reporters, Tillis insisted he’s “not a no” on Blanche. But he said Trump’s $1.8 billion taxpayer-funded slush fund “needs to go away,” and he’s focused on making that happen. So far, Blanche has refused to sign a formal, written guarantee that this fund has been terminated.
“They’re going to hang this yoke around our candidates’ necks, and rightly so,” the North Carolina senator said of voters being strongly opposed to the fund. “The only logical conclusion I can draw from this setback is that, in fact, there is somebody who wants to enable [the slush fund] at the right time. That’s unacceptable.”
Cornyn has been pushing for relatively modest changes to Trump’s audit immunity granted by his settlement. Namely, the Texas Republican wants to ensure it’s only retrospective, not prospective. They have yet to reach an agreement on that, either.
Both senators have political beef with the president. Cornyn, a veteran Senate Republican, overwhelmingly lost his primary in May after Trump endorsed his GOP opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. And Tillis announced last year he wouldn’t seek reelection after the president threatened to endorse a primary challenger against him after Tillis said he couldn’t support the president’s so-called Big Beautiful Bill.
Asked Thursday about some people suggesting his “sour grapes” were part of the reason he was opposing Blanche’s nomination, Tillis scoffed.
“You’re probably talking to a very small percentage of people here whose opinions I could [not] care less about,” the North Carolina senator told reporters. “I’m still working on getting this done, and I’m still optimistic that we will.”
He shrugged when asked if he thinks the president would have a better chance of confirming Blanche next year, when neither Tillis nor Cornyn would be there. Democrats are seen as having an outside shot of winning control of the Senate, and public polling gives Democratic candidates small leads over the GOP nominees to replace both men.
“Well, I guess the president’s going to have to decide what the split looks like,” Tillis said of the Senate’s partisan breakdown.
He slipped into a Senate elevator grumbling about something being “a waste of time.”
Tillis and Cornyn have gotten the most attention for their hangups with Blanche, but that’s namely because their votes are needed on the judiciary panel. There may be other GOP senators who have problems with the president’s attorney general pick, but who are happy to let Cornyn and Tillis field tough questions about him for now.
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) is one of them. He has broken with the president from time to time, and also lost his Republican primary this year to a candidate backed by Trump.
Waiting for a Senate elevator to whisk him away, he stood in silence for several awkward seconds with a grin as a HuffPost reporter asked where he stands on Blanche’s nomination. As he ignored the questions, the reporter tried flashing a thumbs-up or a thumbs-down, looking for any sign of feelings.
The elevator doors closed.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that he may withdraw acting Attorney General Todd Blanche's nomination for the full-time post rather than accept limits sought by Senate Republicans on a tax audit immunity deal that benefits Trump and members of his family. The agreement was negotiated by Trump with his own Department of Justice.
Trump also made clear that he wants Blanche, his former personal lawyer, to remain in charge of the Justice Department. The Senate Judiciary Committee scrapped a planned vote on Thursday to advance Blanche's nomination after hours of negotiations failed to resolve objections from Republican Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis. With all Democratic senators opposed, a single Republican holdout on the committee could block Blanche's confirmation.
Trump, who called Blanche "a STAR", said he would keep him as acting attorney general until Cornyn of Texas and Tillis of North Carolina leave office. "I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd's name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office," Trump posted on his social media site. Cornyn and Tillis have said they will not support Blanche's nomination unless they get written assurances on the settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service over his leaked tax returns. Responding to Trump, Cornyn wrote on social media that the president is "mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis." He later told reporters, "I don't know whether they think they can wait us out or we'll cave, but I assure you we won't."
A major flashpoint in the settlement was the proposed USD 1.8 billion "Anti-Weaponization Fund", which was meant to pay Trump allies who believed they were wronged by the Justice Department. That part was dropped after bipartisan outrage over the possibility that violent January 6 rioters could benefit. Officials have said another part of the settlement remains in place, giving Trump and members of his family immunity from tax audits. Though Blanche has repeatedly said the fund is dead, lawmakers have sought a written commitment, especially as Trump has continued to back the idea.
Another sticking point was the settlement's audit immunity clause, which said the US government is "forever barred and precluded" from scrutinizing or prosecuting Trump, his sons and the Trump Organisation's current and past tax examinations. Cornyn and Tillis want the administration to change the agreement to make clear that it applies only to existing audits and does not shield future tax filings from examination. Tillis described Trump's approach as "win a battle, lose a war." He added, "It makes no sense to me. This is not popular. The president's not winning on this issue. It is killing some of our candidates because they can't explain it. And now, it looks like they weren't being honest when they said it was inoperative." Most Republican senators oppose the settlement, and Trump has also repeatedly targeted Cornyn and Tillis. Tillis had announced last year that he would not seek re-election and has criticised the administration over the pardons of January 6 rioters and other issues.
Even if Trump withdraws Blanche's nomination, the immediate running of the Justice Department may not change much. Blanche can continue either as acting attorney general or as deputy attorney general, the number two post to which he was confirmed last year. In effect, the dispute has left Blanche's confirmation stalled, with Republican senators pressing for changes to the tax settlement while Trump insists he can wait them out.

One problem for Trump in a postponement is that the Senate is currently controlled 53-47 by Republicans but could shift to Democrats in the November midterm elections. Both senators’ seats could be filled by Democrats.
Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, who chairs the Senate Committee on the Judiciary, postponed a committee vote that was scheduled for Thursday morning to advance Blanche’s nomination to the full Senate.

sources.text:
President Trump said Thursday that he might pull Todd Blanche’s nomination as attorney general, after two Republican senators threatened to withhold their support.
“I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing,” Trump posted on Truth Social.
His comments came after the Senate Judiciary Committee postponed a vote Thursday that would have advanced Blanche’s nomination.
Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, one of the key holdout votes, told reporters Wednesday that he had not received a written confirmation from the Department of Justice that it would eliminate provisions in a proposed settlement between Trump and the department over a lawsuit he filed concerning the leak of his tax returns.
The most contentious provisions would have created a $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” for Trump allies and Jan. 6 defendants, and shielded Trump and his family from future audits by the Internal Revenue Service.
“I think they [the administration] realizes that we are serious,” Cornyn, who lost his reelection bid in May after Trump endorsed his opponent, said after canceling an in-person meeting with Blanche.
The committee did not immediately announce a new date for a confirmation vote. Shortly after the postponement, Cornyn said negotiations between the committee members and the DOJ were still ongoing, and that the DOJ had received “some pushbacks” from the White House.
“I thought we were pretty close to landing the plane last night, but this morning there's been some more complications. I think if this were just between me and Todd Blanche, we would have worked this out,” Cornyn added.
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who is not seeking reelection over his disagreement with the Trump administration, has also made clear his opposition to the Anti-Weaponization Fund.
“He [Blanche] is a qualified candidate. We just need to get the issues off the table,” Tillis said on Wednesday.
What happens if Blanche is not confirmed?
Todd Blanche has been serving as acting attorney general for the DOJ since Trump removed Pam Bondi in April over her handling of the Epstein files. Unlike interim U.S. prosecutors, who can lawfully serve 120 days without a Senate confirmation, an acting attorney general can serve for as long as a president wants.
That is because of U.S. Code § 508, which states that “the Deputy Attorney General may exercise all the duties of that office” if the office of Attorney General is vacant and the law does not state a time limit for how long the acting attorney general can legally serve.
The law, which was passed decades before the Federal Vacancies Reform Act (VRA) of 1998, takes legal precedence. While the FVRA generally limits officials serving in a temporary capacity to no longer than 210 days after the position becomes vacant, the law also made exceptions to agency-specific laws that had been previously codified.
A similar arrangement existed under the Biden administration. In 2023, after Marty Walsh resigned as labor secretary, President Biden nominated Julie Su to fill the vacancy. Su, who had served as deputy labor secretary, ultimately failed to get confirmed by the Senate due to the lack of support from Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia and Sen. Kyrsten Sinema of Arizona.
Su served as acting labor secretary for the rest of the Biden administration under a similar statutory provision, despite Republicans' objections. In 2023, the Government Accountability Office, which oversees the federal government’s compliance with vacancy laws, concluded in a letter that time limitations “do not apply” to Su’s case.
What did Blanche say about the demands?
During his confirmation hearing earlier this month, Todd Blanche said the Anti-Weaponization Fund was “dead.”
However, Sen. Cornyn pointed out during the hearing that the settlement agreement made between Trump and the Department of Justice that included the fund could only be modified through “a written agreement” between two parties. When pressed by Cornyn, Blanche said Trump could potentially enforce the agreement if he decides to do so.
“They [Trump’s legal counsel] could say that we breached by not moving forward,” Blanche said.
TIME has also reached out to the Department of Justice for comment.

Cornyn said the Justice Department had not provided the written assurances he demanded that the so-called "anti-weaponization" fund would not move forward, even though Blanche has repeatedly said the fund is dead, including as recently as his July 15 confirmation hearing. As a self-imposed deadline approached Wednesday afternoon, Cornyn challenged reporters to "call over to the Department of Justice and tell them they have one hour and 50 minutes to get me what I asked for." Asked whether the department might be trying to pressure him into backing down, Cornyn told CNN, "Maybe they think they can roll me," before adding flatly, "No." A Justice Department official said the department had provided Cornyn's staff a written proposal the day before "following ongoing discussion with both the Committee and the Senator's office," but Cornyn disputed that characterization and separately accused the department of "stonewalling."
Trump escalated the standoff Thursday in a post on Truth Social, calling Blanche "a STAR" with the potential to become "one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time," while saying Cornyn and Tillis were refusing to vote for the nominee, who would remain acting attorney general regardless. Trump proposed leaving Blanche in the acting role for the coming months and then resubmitting his nomination after Cornyn and Tillis leave the Senate when their current terms end in January. "I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd's name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office," Trump wrote. The president took credit for having "ended" both senators' political careers, noting Cornyn lost his Republican primary in May to Trump-backed challenger and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, while Tillis announced last year he would not seek reelection. Trump also noted that both senators had voted to confirm Merrick Garland, President Biden's attorney general nominee, in a pointed jab at their current holdout.
Cornyn responded that Trump "is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis," suggesting broader unease within the Senate GOP conference over the settlement's terms. The $1.776 billion fund at the center of the dispute was created as part of a settlement tied to a lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS over a 2016 leak of his tax records, and was intended to compensate people who claimed to have been unfairly targeted by politically motivated federal investigations — a group that could potentially include participants in the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot. The fund drew bipartisan criticism after its creation, and the Justice Department told lawmakers earlier this year it was abandoning the plan following a federal judge's order halting related work while legal challenges proceeded. Cornyn and Tillis have pushed for that assurance to be codified in writing rather than left as a verbal commitment, and Cornyn said the department's proposed language sent late Wednesday still did not resolve his concerns.
The Senate Judiciary Committee's 12 Republicans and 10 Democrats mean Blanche cannot advance without near-unanimous GOP support, and every Democrat on the committee is expected to vote against the nomination regardless of the fund dispute. Sen. Cory Booker held a forum earlier this month arguing Blanche is unfit to lead the department, and ranking member Dick Durbin has publicly criticized the nomination in recent days; outside groups including Planned Parenthood and the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law have also filed lobbying disclosures opposing Blanche. Blanche, Trump's former personal attorney, has served as acting attorney general since Trump removed Pam Bondi from the role in April, and his nomination has already drawn scrutiny in both parties over his handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files alongside the IRS settlement dispute.
Trump's threat to pull the nomination rather than negotiate further with Cornyn and Tillis marks a shift from the administration's posture just a day earlier, when officials had signaled openness to further discussion ahead of the postponed vote. That Trump explicitly tied his willingness to wait out the two senators to their impending departure from the Senate suggests he calculates the political cost of a prolonged standoff is lower than the cost of conceding to their demands on the IRS settlement, since neither senator faces reelection consequences that could otherwise pressure the White House to compromise. The president's jab referencing Cornyn and Tillis's past votes for Garland reframes the dispute as a matter of political consistency rather than substance, a framing that sidesteps the specific written-assurance demand both senators say remains unresolved. Cornyn's response, broadening the concern beyond just himself and Tillis, raises the possibility that other Senate Republicans share similar reservations about the settlement even if they have not yet said so publicly. Cornyn's diminished political exposure following his primary loss, and Tillis's decision not to seek reelection, appear to be significant factors enabling both senators to hold out against a sitting president from their own party, a dynamic Trump's own social media post implicitly acknowledged by tying his strategy to their departure dates.
Whether Trump follows through on withdrawing Blanche's nomination, or whether the standoff resolves before Cornyn and Tillis depart in January, will be the central question in the coming weeks. Continued scrutiny of the IRS settlement's terms, the Epstein-files controversy, and whether other Judiciary Committee Republicans signal similar concerns are likely to shape how the confirmation fight unfolds, along with whether Blanche's extended tenure as acting attorney general itself becomes a point of political contention.

The pair have demanded written assurances about the settlement of the president’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. Cornyn recently lost the Republican primary in Texas, and Tillis is not seeking reelection.
Follow along live.
RFK Jr. launches an HHS cooking show — 4:30 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is known for eating a “carnivore” diet of red meat and fermented foods – but he’s broadening those horizons for a new online cooking show.
He and celebrity chef Andrew Gruel prepared crispy salmon cakes and an arugula, apple and white bean salad in the first episode of “The Real Food Show,” posted Thursday with the branding of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
The department says the show will provide examples of nutritious and affordable meals for Americans who want to eat healthier. It comes months after the Trump administration released new dietary guidelines at the start of this year.
Along with Kennedy’s recently launched podcast series, the show promotes some of the more popular aspects of his “Make America Healthy Again” initiative at a time when many have criticized his agenda in other areas, such as vaccines.
Bessent says US expects China to meet rare earth and agriculture commitments — 3:07 p.m.
By the Associated Press
After meeting on Thursday with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on social media that the Trump administration expects Beijing “to fully meet its commitments on rare earths and U.S. agricultural products.” Trade representative Greer also attended, Bessent said.
The meeting between finance and trade officials sets the stage for Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected meeting face to face in September.
Bessent said the group also discussed implementation of the Trade and Investment Boards as a way to build more “balanced, fair, and constructive U.S.-China economic relationship.”
Trump-branded commemorative USA 250 passports to become more widely available — 3:04 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The State Department says its limited-edition Trump-branded commemorative USA 250 passports will soon become available to Americans outside the greater Washington, D.C., area.
Beginning next month, the department’s 27 passport agencies around the nation will start one-day events, offering the so-called “Patriot Passports” that feature a page emblazoned with a stern portrait of Trump. Previously, the commemorative passport had only been available at the Washington, D.C., passport office for in-person applicants.
Starting on Aug. 8, passport offices in seven cities including Chicago, New York City and Dallas will offer the Trump passports. More passport offices will be included throughout August. Applicants wanting the special passport must apply to the selected offices in person on the day specified. Those wanting a traditional passport must apply on different days.
A total of 250,000 of the commemorative passports will be available.
What to know about Trump’s nearly $1.8B fund to compensate allies claiming political targeting — 2:53 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Back in May, the Justice Department announced that allies of the president who believe they have been wrongly investigated and prosecuted could soon have access to a nearly $1.8 billion compensation fund.
Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement that the “Anti-Weaponization Fund” would represent “a lawful process for victims of lawfare and weaponization to be heard and seek redress.” Blanche’s statement made no mention of how investigations and prosecutions of Trump’s political opponents under his watch have exposed the Justice Department to the same claims of politicized law enforcement that he has said he opposed.
The fund was announced as part of a deal to resolve Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service over the leak of his tax returns, but was subsequently scrapped anda federal judge blocked the fund’s creation.
Trump wants more military veterans to become commercial truckers — 2:18 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The president hosted an event on the White House campus where he said America’s road had been “terrorized by unqualified illegal aliens dangerously driving big rigs” and that he would replace these immigrants with “highly qualified American veterans.”
The Trump administration has dubbed this program the “Freedom Haulers Initiative,” under which anyone who has driven a heavy truck for the military would automatically be eligible for a commercial drivers license.
Trump said that 34 states are part of the initiative.
Immigrants account for about 20% of all truck drivers, but all of these non-domiciled licenses for immigrants represent only about 5% of all commercial driver’s licenses, or about 200,000 drivers.
Trump administration is ending a Medicare drug subsidy program — 2:14 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Millions of older adults on Medicare prescription drug coverage could face steeper monthly costs in 2027, after the Trump administration concludes a temporary subsidy program that has helped offset premiums for the past two years.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services this week announced it would wrap up the program, which was initially implemented by the Biden administration in 2024 to lower patients’ Medicare Part D prescription drug costs in response to effects of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act.
While federal officials insist the financial impact on Medicare beneficiaries will be minimal, the decision opens the Republican-led administration to potential political consequences in a high-stakes midterm election year. Voters have identified cost of living as a top concern, and many older adults, who tend to vote in high numbers, are on fixed incomes where every dollar counts.
The roughly 25 million Americans with Medicare Part D plans will find out about their 2027 rates in the fall, when they are casting ballots in November’s elections.
State Department says ‘unfortunate error’ led to badly mislabeled map of Africa at AIDS conference — 2:10 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The State Department is taking full responsibility for a badly mislabeled map of Africa that was presented at a global
AIDS conference last week in Brazil.
It called it an “unfortunate error” that should not take away from the Trump administration’s commitment to fighting the deadly virus.
“This was an unfortunate error caused by a team member who hastily altered the slide deck immediately before the presentation at the AIDS 2026 Conference,” the State Department said Thursday after photos of the map were posted online by conference participants.
A photo of the map was shared by AIDS activist Emily Bass in a Substack post on Sunday showing six countries mislabeled. Among them, Nigeria was placed in roughly the same location as Niger; Ivory Coast, placed in southern Africa; Mozambique, placed in the Horn of Africa; and Cameroon, placed in what appeared to be the location of Ghana. The State Department confirmed that six countries had been misidentified.
Senate rejects another war powers resolution to halt Iran war — 1:33 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Most Senate Republicans voted against advancing the measure in the Democrats’ latest effort to end Trump’s engagement in military action without congressional approval.
“We were told this president would bring peace and lower prices,” said Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who sponsored the resolution. “What is President Trump doing? Pouring bills of tax dollars into an open-ended war with Iran.”
The tally was 49-50. Three Republicans, Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, joined most Democrats to advance the measure. Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania joined Republicans to oppose.
Since the war began earlier this year, House and Senate Democrats have introduced more than a dozen war powers resolutions, but none has passed both chambers.
Trump administration wants veterans to replace immigrant truck drivers who lost licenses — 1:28 p.m.
By the Associated Press
The White House is encouraging veterans who drove large military vehicles to consider a career in trucking.
Attracting more veterans to trucking will help replace immigrant drivers who lost their commercial driver’s licenses during the crackdown over the past year. The administration enforced English-proficiency requirements and worked to ensure drivers were qualified to pilot 80,000-pound trucks.
Veterans who drove trucks or other large vehicles in the military recently will be eligible to skip the skills test when they apply for a commercial driver’s license. Trump plans to highlight the campaign Thursday afternoon at the White House.
Trucking groups like the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association support getting more veterans into trucking. Roughly 40% of that group’s 150,000 members are veterans.
“Military veterans have the skills to succeed in trucking, and that’s what makes them the safest operators of the 80,000-pound commercial vehicles that traverse America’s roadways,” said Todd Spencer, who is president of that trucking trade group.
Cornyn, Tillis react to Trump saying he may withdraw Blanche’s nomination — 1:00 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Republican Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis have said they won’t back Blanche’s nomination without additional assurances spelling an end to a proposed $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” created to resolve President Trump’s lawsuit against the IRS over the leak of his tax returns.
The two senators have also pressed Trump’s administration to modify the tax immunity agreement to make clear that it covers only existing audits and does not protect the president from examination of future tax filings.
Tillis characterized the president’s position as “win a battle, lose a war.”
“It makes no sense to me,” Tillis said. “This is not popular. The president’s not winning on this issue. It is killing some of our candidates because they can’t explain it. And now, it looks like they weren’t being honest when they said it was inoperative.”
“I don’t know whether they think they can wait us out or we’ll cave, but I assure you we won’t,” Cornyn said Thursday of the Trump administration. In a social media post responding to Trump, Cornyn wrote that the president is “mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis.”
Why Republicans aren’t funding a key Senate race yet — 12:36 p.m.
By the New York Times
In one of this year’s most competitive Senate races, Republicans are refusing to spend money -- so far.
That peculiar dynamic is playing out in Texas, where the fate of the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, will help decide which party controls the U.S. Senate. But Paxton has struggled to raise cash, and no one has stepped in yet to help him.
Paxton finds himself in a unique situation among Senate candidates, according to interviews with a dozen Republicans with ties to his campaign. Republican donors still hold grudges from a bruising primary. The state, with its 18-plus television markets, is an epically expensive setting. And his Democratic opponent, James Talarico, has proved to be a particularly strong fundraiser.
Perhaps the most striking piece of Paxton’s money woes is the high-stakes game of chicken that two of the Republican Party’s biggest money committees, along with their allied donors, are playing.
Democratic senators call on Treasury to move forward with new Tubman $20 bill — 12:24 p.m.
By the Associated Press
Ten Democratic senators are calling on Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to provide more details about whether a longtime effort to place Harriet Tubman’s likeness on the $20 bill has been canceled or merely delayed.
The senators are following up on comments Bessent made to Spectrum News, saying Treasury was “not at present” planning to put Tubman on the $20 bill.
The senators in their letter are calling on Bessent to immediately reconsider and resume plans to create the new bill. They are also asking for a briefing on the matter. Meanwhile, the senators noted that Treasury has prepared the design for a $250 bill featuring Trump.
The effort to place the 19th-century abolitionist leader on the $20 bill began more than a decade ago, was delayed during Trump’s first term and restarted during former President Joe Biden’s presidency.
Trump says he may delay Blanche nomination until dissenting senators leave office — 11:38 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Trump says he may withdraw Todd Blanche’s nomination as attorney general until Republican senators who are seeking concessions from the top prosecutor leave office next year.
Trump doubled down Thursday on choosing his former personal lawyer as the nation’s top lawman, calling him “a STAR.” He said he’ll keep Blanche as acting attorney general until Republican Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis are gone.
Cornyn and Tillis have demanded additional assurances in writing that the “Anti-Weaponization Fund” is dead and have pressed for clarification on the scope of a tax immunity deal Trump secured by suing the Internal Revenue Service. Cornyn has said he wants the administration to modify that piece of the settlement to make clear that it covers only existing audits and does not protect the president from examination of future tax filings.
Trump’s comments came after the Senate Judiciary Committee postponed a planned vote on Thursday to advance Blanche’s nomination.
Senate committee advances nomination of Dr. Erica Schwartz to be Trump’s CDC director — 10:53 a.m.
By the Associated Press
A Senate committee on Thursday advanced Dr. Erica Schwartz’s nomination to be director of the nation’s top public health agency, setting aside concerns that she won’t stand up to political meddling.
If confirmed by the full Senate, the 54-year-old would become the 22nd director of the Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which is charged with protecting Americans from preventable health threats. Her resume includes medical and law degrees, a stint as deputy surgeon general, and a leadership position at the U.S. Coast Guard.
Schwartz appeared to be on shaky ground after Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., and others questioned whether she would be willing to stand up to Robert F. Kennedy Jr., if the health secretary ordered CDC to do something unsupported by science and good public health practice. But Cassidy later expressed confidence that “she knows what she’s doing.”
Trump touted his tariffs in Michigan despite rising costs. Even some of his supporters are worried. — 10:47 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Flying to a rally at General Motors this week, the president declared that “car companies are doing better than they’ve ever done” thanks to his tariffs, “All because of Trump.”
“It’s amazing what tariffs will do for General Motors” the Republican leader said before autographing a white Corvette. “Michigan is thriving,” he told cheering supporters.
That’s not exactly true, according to many metrics. Tariffs have cost businesses in Michigan and across the country billions of dollars while stoking inflation that continues to run hot. Many Americans believe tariffs have pushed prices higher and the war in Iran has increased gasoline prices, hurting consumer confidence in the economy while keeping Trump’s approval ratings low.
There are few places where Trump’s boasts and economic reality are more likely to collide ahead of November’s midterm elections than in battleground Michigan, which holds its primary on Tuesday.
US-Iran conflict enters new phase as Saudi Arabia helps hit proxies and diplomacy stalls again — 10:40 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The stop-start fighting between the United States and Iran appears to have entered a new phase with Saudi Arabia publicly joining military escalations against Tehran-backed proxies and an already untenable diplomatic effort to end the war faltering once again.
Little is clear about what strategy, if any, American or Iranian officials have for a path forward. The Republican president has vacillated for months between insisting a deal was near to end the war and Tehran’s nuclear program, and using vulgarities and threats to try to get Iran to capitulate.
The stakes for continued U.S. military action have never been higher for Trump and his party as the conflict, unpopular among many Americans, has jolted the world economy months before voters get their say in November. The renewed fighting has killed and injured more American troops and raised concerns about drawing down the stockpiles of key U.S. air defense systems.
US economy turns in sluggish 1.5 percent second-quarter growth and inflation remains above Fed target — 9:03 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The U.S. economy expanded at a sluggish 1.5% pace from April through June as rising imports weighed on growth. But consumer spending rose. And the Federal Reserve’s favored measure of inflation grew more slowly last month, by 3.7%, but remained above the central bank’s 2% target.
The Commerce Department reported Thursday that growth in U.S. gross domestic product — the nation’s output of goods and services — decelerated from 2.1% in the first three months of 2026 and came in below economists’ expectations.
The Fed on Wednesday chose to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged for the fifth straight meeting. But three regional Fed presidents dissented, saying they wanted to raise rates to combat elevated inflation.
Higher costs have frustrated Americans ahead of November’s midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump’s Republicans keep full control of Congress.
US filings for jobless benefits rise to 197,000 last week, but layoffs remain historically low — 8:59 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The number of Americans applying for unemployment benefits rose last week but layoffs remain in the historically healthy range of the past few years.
U.S. filings for jobless aid in the week ending July 25 rose by 9,000 to 197,000, the Labor Department reported Thursday. The previous week’s figure was revised up by 1,000 to 188,000 but remains the lowest in more than 50 years.
Analysts surveyed by the data firm FactSet forecast 207,000 new applications.
Weekly filings for unemployment benefits are considered representative of layoffs and are close to a real-time indicator of the health of the U.S. job market.
How views on Trump’s handling of Iran have shifted, according to a new poll — 5:35 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Most Americans say the war in Iran has not been worth fighting, and President Trump’s approval rating on Iran has fallen slightly since last month, according to a new AP-NORC poll.
The results are a stark repudiation of Trump’s approach to the conflict, which has dragged on far longer than he originally predicted.
About two-thirds of US adults say the war with Iran, which began Feb. 28, has not been worthwhile, according to the new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. That includes the vast majority of Democrats and independents, as well as about 37 percent of Republicans.
Urban League report says Trump administration is harming Black Americans’ chances at American Dream — 3:13 a.m.
By the Associated Press
The American Dream may not be dead for many Black Americans, but it is further away than at any point since the Civil Rights Movement, warns a report by the National Urban League.
Released on Thursday, the annual “State of Black America” report grimly describes Black Americans ' economic and political prospects as having worsened due to policy changes from President Trump’s administration, according to a copy obtained by The Associated Press.
The report contends that the challenges it highlights for Black communities are warning signs for the prosperity of all Americans.
Trump touted his tariffs in Michigan despite rising costs. Even some of his supporters are worried. — 12:11 a.m.
By the Associated Press
Flying to a rally at General Motors this week, President Trump declared that “car companies are doing better than they’ve ever done” thanks to his tariffs.
“All because of Trump,” he said.
It was a message the president repeated while touring a collection of new vehicles, predicting that “it’s amazing what tariffs will do for General Motors” before autographing a white Corvette commemorating America’s 250th anniversary. He later told a crowd of cheering supporters that “Michigan is thriving.”

sources.news_title: Trump may pull Blanche nomination. What's Plan B?
sources.text:
President Donald Trump suggested Thursday that he may temporarily withdraw Todd Blanche's nomination for attorney general as Republican Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina continue to withhold support, signaling a potential setback for one of his highest-profile nominees.
Cornyn and Tillis, both of whom are set to leave office next year, have demanded written assurances that a controversial "Anti-Weaponization Fund" tied to Trump's settlement with the Internal Revenue Service will be permanently terminated.
Their opposition forced the Senate Judiciary Committee to postpone a planned vote Thursday on Blanche's nomination. The two Republicans have said they will not support advancing the nomination until they receive written commitments from Blanche regarding the settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the IRS, which included provisions shielding the president and certain family members from future tax audits.
In a Truth Social post, Trump said he would have "no objection" to pulling Blanche's name and resubmitting it after the senators leave office. The president added that Blanche would remain in charge of the Department of Justice in an acting capacity, raising fresh questions about the department's long-term leadership if the confirmation fight remains stalled.
The president posted, "Todd Blanche is a STAR, and everyone knows it! He has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time. However, John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting. Remember, both Cornyn and Tillis voted for Merrick Garland, and others, too numerous to mention. I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office. President DONALD J. TRUMP"
Following the president's post, Cornyn countered on X, "POTUS is mistaken if he believes concerns about the provisions in his tax lawsuit settlement are limited to me and Senator Tillis"
Tillis dismissed Trump's threat and suggested the president was being poorly advised as the standoff over Blanche's nomination continued. Speaking to reporters, the North Carolina Republican said Trump should listen to those who believe the disputed fund should be made "completely dead," rather than leave open the possibility of reviving it in the future. Tillis added that "the president's getting bad advice" from advisers who want to "bring it back to life at some point."
How Blanche's Confirmation Fight Reached a Breaking Point
After Attorney General Pam Bondi's departure from the Justice Department in April, Trump moved quickly to install her deputy, Blanche, a former federal prosecutor and longtime ally who had represented him in several high-profile legal cases. Blanche was elevated to acting attorney general and later tapped to lead the department permanently, setting up what many Republicans initially expected to be a smooth confirmation process.
That expectation changed after scrutiny intensified around the administration's settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the IRS. The agreement resolved a long-running dispute over the alleged disclosure of Trump's tax information, but some lawmakers raised concerns about provisions included in the deal and the broader precedent it could set.
Questions also emerged about an associated "Anti-Weaponization Fund" established as part of the settlement. Critics argued the arrangement lacked sufficient guardrails, prompting calls for greater transparency about how any remaining funds would be handled and whether the program would continue.
Those concerns eventually centered on Blanche's nomination. Cornyn and Tillis, both members of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said during Blanche's confirmation hearing that they wanted stronger assurances from the nominee before supporting his advancement, turning what had largely been viewed as a procedural confirmation process into a high-profile intra-party dispute.
The standoff came to a head this week as negotiations between Blanche, the senators and committee leaders continued behind the scenes. With the votes not yet secured, the Judiciary Committee delayed a planned confirmation vote, leaving the nomination in limbo and increasing pressure on the White House to find a path forward.
Blanche has also faced scrutiny from some Republicans over the Justice Department's handling of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The issue became a flashpoint inside Trump's political coalition after the administration declined to release additional materials that some supporters had expected would become public.
Trump's latest comments suggest he is now weighing alternatives if the impasse persists, including keeping Blanche at the helm of the department in an acting capacity while postponing a full Senate confirmation fight until a later date.
Midterm Stakes Loom Over GOP Infighting
Delaying Blanche's confirmation until after Cornyn and Tillis leave office could carry risks of its own. Republicans are defending competitive open-seat races in both Texas and North Carolina, and if the party loses its Senate majority in the midterms, Blanche could find himself facing a far more difficult path to confirmation.
In Texas, Trump backed Attorney General Ken Paxton's successful primary challenge against Cornyn, helping drive the incumbent from the race. Paxton now faces Democratic state Representative James Talarico in a contest that has drawn national attention and is viewed as one of the GOP's most vulnerable Senate defenses. Recent polling and fundraising reports have suggested a competitive race, raising concerns among Republicans about holding the seat.
North Carolina presents a similar challenge. Tillis' retirement created an open-seat race that both parties view as critical to determining Senate control. The contest features former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee, and former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley, a Trump ally who secured the GOP nomination. With Democrats viewing North Carolina as one of their best pickup opportunities and several forecasters rating the race as highly competitive, Republican leaders are under pressure to avoid intraparty divisions that could complicate their path to retaining the seat.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Sam Wilson.

Trump threatens to pull Todd Blanche’s AG nomination rather than give in to Republican holdouts over weaponization fund
President vows to resubmit his ex-lawyer’s nomination once Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis are no longer in office next year
President Donald Trump on Thursday said he would consider withdrawing Todd Blanche’s nomination to be the next U.S. Attorney General rather than concede to demands from two Republican senators who want him to guarantee in writing that he’s given up plans to use $1.8 billion in tax dollars to reward criminals who were prosecuted during previous Democratic administrations.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump called his ex-criminal defense attorney Blanche a “star” who “has the potential to go down as one of the Greatest Attorney Generals of All Time” while grousing that Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas and Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., are “refusing to vote” for Blanche’s confirmation. He also vowed to keep Blanche in place as acting attorney general regardless of what the Senate does with his nomination.
“I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office,” Trump posted.
Both Cornyn and Tillis are in their last year of service in the upper chamber — the Texas senator lost a primary after Trump backed his challenger, state AG Ken Paxton, while Tillis elected to retire rather than face a Trump-backed MAGA insurgent over his past criticism of the president.
The two outgoing Republicans have for days been pushing Blanche and the White House to provide assurances that Trump’s plan for a $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization fund” are permanently dead before they will give their assent to his bid to replace former attorney general Pam Bondi, also a former Trump personal lawyer, on a permanent basis.
Both are members of the Senate Judiciary Committee, which had been set to vote to advance the nomination at a meeting on Thursday before it became clear that the panel would not be able to do so without support from both.
A committee spokesperson said on Wednesday that the hearing had been “postponed as work continues to secure sufficient support in committee to favorably report Attorney General-nominee Todd Blanche, who is highly qualified for the job.”
While the White House and Blanche have both stated that the fund is “dead,” Cornyn and Tillis have both asked for assurances in writing out of concern that the text of a settlement with the president’s legal team still could require it to be set up — as well as fears that Blanche and the White House cannot be trusted on this matter.
They also oppose a provision giving Trump perpetual immunity from IRS audits of his finances prior to May 19, 2026.
Cornyn told MS NOW on Thursday he was “prepared to vote no” on the president’s pick.
“But I do think I owe it to my constituents and to Mr. Blanche to try to negotiate in good faith, and that's what we've been doing,” he said.
Cornyn added that Trump “could fix this in a minute” by providing the written assurances he and Tillis have demanded.
The so-called “weaponization fund” at issue was birthed from a settlement between Trump’s legal team and the IRS the Department of Justice engineered after Trump took office in 2025. In a press release, the DoJ claimed that the fund would be used to “provide a systematic process to hear and redress claims of others who suffered weaponization and lawfare” allegedly committed by the agency.
The plan was met with immediate revulsion in Congress, with moderate Republicans in both chambers joining with Democrats to condemn it and describe it as a “slush fund” designed to reward Trump’s allies with lucrative payouts.
Controversy immediately erupted over whether the funds could be used to reward January 6 rioters who were successfully prosecuted by the Biden Justice Department, then pardoned by Trump after he took office.
Funding for it was left out of the Republicans’ second reconciliation package last month, but Cornyn and his holdout colleagues have gone further by demanding it be written out of existence altogether.
In his Truth Social post, Trump claimed credit for ending both Cornyn’s and Tillis’ political careers, implying that both were opposing Blanche out of pique.
But the Texas senator noted he’s voted with Trump “99.3 percent of the time” and said the president’s decision to endorse his primary opponent “has nothing to do” with his opposition to Blanche absent a resolution on the “weaponization fund.”
“This is about making sure that even if you're the president of the United States, you don't get favorable terms from the government in a settlement of a lawsuit that ordinary citizens would not get, like protections from audits by the IRS for the foreseeable future,” he said.
John Bowden contributed reporting from Washington
